entries.title: Jürgen Klopp starts Germany job with shaky Netherlands draw
entries.summary: A late Netherlands goal denied Jürgen Klopp a win in his first match as Germany coach. The former Liverpool and Borussia Dortmund boss has big ambitions, but the game showed he's going to need more time to achieve them.

entries.title: UNGA: Gaza dominates agenda as Abbas, Netanyahu speak
entries.summary: Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu called accusing Israel of genocide in Gaza the "greatest lie of the century." Many delegates walked out for his General Assembly speech. Mahmoud Abbas also spoke earlier. DW has more.
entries.content:
Published September 22, 2026last updated September 25, 2026

Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu called accusing Israel of genocide in Gaza the "greatest lie of the century." Many delegates walked out for his General Assembly speech. Mahmoud Abbas also spoke earlier. DW has more.

Skip next section What you need to know

What you need to know

  • Israel's Prime Minister said attacking Iran was one of his 'easiest' decisions, as he had no real choice
  • Many representatives walked out of the UN General Assembly ahead of Benjamin Netanyahu's speech
  • Palestinian President Mahmoud Abbas earlier urged nations to support the two-state solution, and sharply criticized Israel and the US
  • The UK will host a meeting on the future of the Gaza Strip, while Saudi Arabia and Norway have called a ministerial meeting to discuss the implementation of the so-called two-state solution
  • Beyond the Middle East, day 3 of the UNGA will address the problem that rising sea levels pose for low-lying islands and coastal regions

Read below for all the top headlines, videos and analyses on the 81 UN General Assembly from September 22-28, 2026:

Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add us as a Preferred Source on Google. Then tap the "Star" or "Preferred" to keep DW News at the top of your feed.

Skip next section That's a wrap on Day 3 of UNGA

That's a wrap on Day 3 of UNGA

We're wrapping up for the day, with the third day's sessions of the 81st General Assembly now complete.

Gaza dominated the speeches today.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu addressed the assembly, denying that his country's actions in Gaza amount to genocide, an accusation leveled by several speakers on Thursday, including Palestinian Prime Minister Mahmoud Abbas.

Several delegates exited the hall as the Israeli prime minister began his speech.

Protesters had also gathered outside the UN Headquarters in New York ahead of Netanyahu's address, with some being arrested.

Before the session wrapped up, the representatives of Iran, Turkey and Qatar used their right of reply to lambast Netanyahu's address.

Join us on Friday, when Iraq, Lebanon, Pakistan, Egypt, Mexico, Haiti, Norway, Sweden and others are due to address the assembly.

Skip next section Nepal's leader says his country is paying the price of climate change

Nepal's leader says his country is paying the price of climate change

Four weeks after catastrophic flash floods ravaged Nepal, the small Himalayan country's young prime minister stood at the podium of the UN General Assembly to warn leaders about the impact of a warming world.

"I wish I could stand here today simply to speak about development, democracy, peace and the hopes of a young nation. Instead, I must speak about death and destruction of epic proportions," said Balendra Shah as he began his address to the UNGA on Thursday.

Nepal's leader calls for international cooperation for protecting the Himalayas

The Nepalese leader stressed that the perils of climate change transcend national borders as he made a case for greater international cooperation for protecting the Himalayas.

"The Himalayas are not peripheral to the planet. They are part of the planet's life-support system," Shah said, proposing the establishment of a "Himalayan Climate Resilience Mechanism," which he said would be led by Nepal, India and China.

Shah elaborated that the mechanism would help countries share satellite data and expertise, as well as monitor glacial lakes that pose a threat. He also called for stronger joint early-warning systems and coordinated, cross-border assistance in the event of a disaster. 

"Let the Himalayas become a laboratory of international cooperation, rather than a frontier of fragmented information," the prime minister said.

Nepal's leader says his country is paying the price of climate change

Shah noted that his country only contributes less than 0.1% of global greenhouse gas emissions.

"We did not create this crisis. Yet we are paying a colossal price for it," he said, adding that he wasn not blaming any nation or continent.

"We are not here to turn climate change into another geopolitical battlefield. We are here to ask everyone to recommit to shared responsibility and solidarity," Shah said.

Nepal seeks grants, not loans, for flood recovery

The Nepalese prime minister emphasized the principles of "Responsibility, Reparation and Resilience" as he called for grant-based support rather than loans.

Shah said that vulnerable nations should not be forced to take on additional debt to recover from climate catastrophes.

"When a climate-driven disaster destroys the infrastructure of a poor country, the answer cannot simply be another mega loan or a patchwork of small grants. We need adequate grant-based support from the world," he said.

36-year-old Shah was theyoungest head of government to speak at the 81st session of the UNGA.

Skip next section 'Hands off ICC,' Dutch PM says amid growing US pressure

'Hands off ICC,' Dutch PM says amid growing US pressure

Netherlands Prime Minister Rob Jetten, addressing the General Assembly on Thursday, said the International Criminal Court, which is based in The Hague, was "under attack."

Jetten did not name the US or President Donald Trump, who on Tuesday urged countries to leave the court, the latest move in his administration's campaign against the ICC.

"How can you possibly be opposed to prosecuting the very worst crimes?" Jetten asked the assembly, drawing loud applause from the delegates.

"I believe there can be only one response. To say: hands off the ICC, and all those other institutions that protect the international legal order. Because the reality is that we still need to fight impunity."

Washington has imposed financial sanctions and visa bans on ICC staff, with officials reportedly preparing additional sanctions that could curtail the court's ability to operate.

Skip next section Yemen, Kuwait stress freedom of navigation at UNGA

Yemen, Kuwait stress freedom of navigation at UNGA

Yemen and Kuwait, both heavily impacted by the Iran war and its regional spillover, have used their General Assembly addresses to stress the importance of the freedom and safety of navigation, while condemning Iran and its proxies in the region.

Abdullah Abdulkader Al Alimi-Bawzer, vice resident of Yemen's Presidential Leadership Council, represents the internationally recognized government, which has been at war with the Iran-backed Houthirebels for more than a decade.

Alimi-Bawzer devoted his address to highlighting recent Houthi actions and their impact on global trade.

The Houthis' conflict with Saudi Arabia, which has led a coalition against them, has recently escalated, with the Yemeni rebels declaring a blockade on Saudi shipping in the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, a crucial global shipping route. This has further squeezed the Saudi kingdom as Iran continues to block access through the Strait of Hormuz.

"Ensuring security at sea begins with eliminating the source of the threat on land," Alimi-Bawzer said, in an apparent reference to the Houthis.

Kuwaiti Crown Prince Sheikh Sabah Khaled Al-Hamad Al-Sabah stressed that freedom and safety of navigation, as well as the right of passage through the Straits of Hormuz and Bab el-Mandeb, must be guaranteed.

"To inflict harm on the economies of the region and the world, and to disrupt global trade and oil markets, Iran is obstructing maritime navigation and closing the Strait of Hormuz, using it as a bargaining chip in the war, in violation of international law and relevant Security Council resolutions," he said.

Kuwait has been among the countries targeted by Iranian strikes since the start of the war, in retaliation for US and Israeli strikes. 

Skip next section Nigeria says don't 'surrender our technological future to paranoia'

Nigeria says don't 'surrender our technological future to paranoia'

Nigeria's Vice President Kashim Shettima addressed the assembly on behalf of President Bola Tinubu.

Among a range of issues, he weighed in on the question of AI with an appeal for an optimistic and proactive approach more than what he deemed undue caution.

"We refuse to surrender our technological future to paranoia," he said. "An invention can be destructive or beneficial, depending on the purpose it serves and the judgment of those who use it. A knife can take a life in the hands of an assailant, and can save one in the hands of a surgeon."

He said that while AI could be used to wage war, it could also "transform" an array of areas like healthcare, education and agriculture.

"Muhc of the anxiety surrounding AI reflects the distrust we have allowed to grow amongst us," Shettima said.

He said Nigeria wished to invite the world "to work with our inventive, resourceful and enterprising young people to direct AI towards humanity's advancement rather than its destruction."

Skip next section Fiji calls for cheaper financial transfers for remittances, saying 'they are not aid'

Fiji calls for cheaper financial transfers for remittances, saying 'they are not aid'

Fijian President Ratu Naiqama Tawakecolati Lalabalavu addressed the chamber on behalf of one of the low-lying island nations at severe risk from climate change on Thursday.

He said that many of the UN's sustainable development goals remained off track with 2030 approaching and said that aid and financial assistance often did a poor job of reaching remote islands exposed to more natural disasters than average. But then he called for a wider financial system that would better enable Fijians to help themselves.

"There is one measure of delivery that reaches Fijian households directly," he said. "Remittances are now Fiji's third-largest source of foreign exchange."

Lalabalavu said these funds paid for school fees, rebuilt homes after cyclones and sustained families between harvests.

"Your excellencies, they are not aid. They are earnings of Fijians abroad, sent home. Yet Pacific corridors remain among the most expensive in the world through which to send money."

He noted how the chamber had in May committed to work to keep such transfer costs below 3% and to eliminate corridors costing more than 5% — he said that Pacific countries like Fiji wanted this to be "treated as an obligation and not an aspiration."

"Labor mobility must also not become a one-way transfer of the people that we have trained," the president said. "Fiji does not begrudge any Fijian the chance to build a life abroad. We ask only that those recruit our nurses, our teachers invest in the systems that recruited them."

Lalabalavu also alluded to Fiji recently declaring a national HIV emergencyand said that organized crime and drug trafficking was exacerbating this problem. He said that as a small impoverished country, Fiji had three requests for the international community:

"That treatment and diagnostics reach small states at prices we can pay. That the Global Fund and UNAIDS be resources at a level that does not force triage between regions, and that our partners treat Pacific narcotics interdiction as the shared security interest it is."

Skip next section Netanyahu calls genocide allegations 'the greatest lie of the century'

Netanyahu calls genocide allegations 'the greatest lie of the century'

The Israeli prime minister said allegations of genocide in Gaza leveled at Israel by various world leaders or groups were false.

"It will take time for the world to acknowledge what is so plain to see. That Hamas used Palestinian civilians as human shields. That it used hospitals, schools, mosques as terrorist command posts. That it sold much of the food we let into Gaza," Netanyahu alleged. 

"And while Hamas did everything possible to keep Palestinians in harm's way — often at gunpoint — Israel did everything possible to get them out of harm's way," he said, listing measures like warnings to civilians.

"I want to ask you a question: what genocidal regime gives a million polio vaccinations to the enemy's population? What genocidal regime enables the distribution of 2 million tons of food into Gaza? Accusing Israel of genocide is the greatest lie of the century," he said.

He also called out New York's "antisemitic" mayor, Zohran Mamdani, as one of the people spreading this message. He said that since Mamdani's election "many Jews no longer feel safe in New York." 

Netanyahu said the "simple truth" was not that Israel committed genocide but that it prevented one, saying "that's exactly what Mr. Mamdani's Hamas buddies would have done to us if we had not stopped them."

Skip next section Netanyahu says he 'drew a red line' on same podium 14 years ago

Netanyahu says he 'drew a red line' on same podium 14 years ago

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu began his speech with a reference to his notorious General Assembly appearance in 2012, when he stood with illustrated graphics depicting how near to creating a nuclear bomb he thought Iran was. 

"Ladies and gentlemen, 14 years ago I stood on this podium and I drew a red line," he said. "I vowed to prevent Iran's murderous dictatorship from developing atomic bombs. Nuclear weapons that could destroy the state of Israel, nuclear weapons that could threaten the whole world. That's exactly what we did."

Netanyahu said that while it was "very hard" to devastate Iran's nuclear facilities, he said it was "one of the easiest decisions" he'd had to make as prime minister, "because if we hadn't done it, we'd all be dead."

Iran contends that its nuclear program was for peaceful purposes like electricity generation, a claim that Israel and the US dispute.

Netanyahu also referred to Syrian President Ahmad al-Sharaa's call for Israel to pull back its forces in the Golan Heights border area, addressing al-Sharaa and saying "you should know that the Jews have been in the Golan Heights since the days of Moses," referring to the Old Testament prophet thought to have lived more than 3,000 years ago.

Skip next section Delegates leave the chamber in large group as Netanyahu enters

Delegates leave the chamber in large group as Netanyahu enters

As Israeli Prime Minster Benjamin Netanyahu's turn to speak at the UN General Assembly came, a large number of delegates from various countries stood up and left the chamber to cheers and jeering.

Only after repeated appeals for calm was it possible for him to begin his address.

"Before I begin, just a quick announcement: if there any other moral cowards who have not yet left this hall, please do so now. Thank you very much," Netanyahu said.

He returned to the issue of the walkout later when discussing his decision to target Iran and its nuclear capabilities.

"Now do you want to hear the ultimate irony? In defending itself, Israel is also defending many of the countries whose delegates just left this hall. In fact, I want you to know that many of their leaders even thank us privately for taking out Iran's nukes," he claimed, saying "it's hard to imagine more mind-blowing hypocrisy."

Protesters had also gathered outside the building in New York ahead of Netanyahu's address. Some were arrested by police. A Democratic nominee for New York's 10th congressional district in November's midterm elections, Brad Lander, also joined the demonstrators, albeit wearing a suit and tie rather than a slogan-laden T-shirt.

Skip next section READ: Nigeria and US sign mining deal

READ: Nigeria and US sign mining deal

On the sidelines of the UN General Assembly, Nigeria and the United States agreed to increase American investiment in the West African nation's mining sector.

Nigeria's Minister for Solid Minerals Dele Alake announced the deal on Thursday, a day after he signed the framework deal with US Deputy Secretary of State Christopher Landau.

"Nigeria cannot remain a source of raw materials while others capture most of the value. We want more local processing, quality jobs, stronger skills and greater opportunities for Nigerian businesses," Alake said.

Read more about the US-Nigeria mining agreement.

Skip next section Abbas calls for saving two-state solution and Palestinian self-determination

Abbas calls for saving two-state solution and Palestinian self-determination

Palestinian President Mahmoud Abbas used his remarks to implore nations to support the two-state solution, saying his people seek a non-militarized, democratic Palestinian state that can exist alongside Israel in peace.

He said the first step to preserving the idea of such a solution is to protect the lands upon which a future Palestinian state would be based, as well as protecting those people who have lived upon them for generations.

Abbas underscored the fact that the Palestinian people would not be displaced by "military occupation, nor settlement expansion, annexation, nor settler terrorism."

He further said that "no lasting security can be built upon the occupation of another people and the denial of its legitimate rights," adding that the Palestinians have their own plans for an independent state and emphasizing the need to end the Israeli occupation in order to negotiate a solution.

This plan, Abbas said, is based on protecting Palestinians from displacement, preserving their lands, democratically renewing political institutions and building a new sovereign Palestinian state — with east Jerusalem as its capital.

All of this, he said, would be carried out with a "commitment to international law" and the right to exercise self-determination with the aim of achieving security and peace with Israel to, "pave the way to regional integration, cooperation, prosperity and security for everyone."

Abbas concluded his remarks by thanking those 160 nations whom he said have recognized Palestinian statehood, calling for its inclusion in the United Nations.

Skip next section Palestinian leader Abbas blasts US and Israel in General Assembly

Palestinian leader Abbas blasts US and Israel in General Assembly

Palestinian President Mahmoud Abbas, addressing those gathered at the UNGA via video because the US State Department refused to allow the Palestinian delegation into the country, has rejected Washington's approach as "unlawful and punitive."

Abbas described the denial of visas as a US failure to live up to its responsibility as the host nation of the international body.

Abbas quickly pivoted to blast Israel's "genocidal war" in Gaza, as well as the sanctioned "ethnic cleansing" perpetrated by Israeli settlers in the occupied West Bank.

Saying that Israeli violations of international law put the two-state solution at grave risk, Abbas described the situation in Gaza, the West Bank and east Jerusalem as part of a "malicious colonial scheme" and warned of a "new Nakba."

He also referenced attacks on Muslim and Christian religious sites by radical Jews as having the potential to transform the current security situation into a wider religiously fueled conflict.

Skip next section Not only Middle East, rising sea level threat also on slate for day 3 meetings

Not only Middle East, rising sea level threat also on slate for day 3 meetings

Beyond AI and the headline-grabbing conflict in the Middle East, the United Nations General Assembly on Thursday will discuss another pressing issue that impacts the world’s citizens — rising sea levels.

A high-level meeting is slated to begin at 10:00 a.m. (1400 GMT) on Thursday as swelling seas redraw coastlines and pose existential risks for islanders and those who live in low-lying areas near the shores of the world's oceans and seas.

The UN says nearly 900 million people live in such areas, adding that another one million could be impacted by mid-century.

Rising sea levels, says the UN, threaten not only land but also livelihoods and even the existence of entire nations. In the words of UN Secretary General Antonio Guterres, "Rising seas are sinking futures."

Skip next section Israeli and Palestinian leaders set to address UNGA on day 3

Israeli and Palestinian leaders set to address UNGA on day 3

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Palestinian President Mahmoud Abbas are both expected to address members of the UN General Assembly (UNGA) on Thursday, with the issue of the Middle East writ large on the day 3 agenda.

Netanyahu, who is increasingly unpopular at home and abroad, will not meet with US officials or Arab leaders during his stay. His office cited a "tight schedule" as the reason, listing as many as nine meetings during his visit, including with the presidents of Argentina and Bolivia, the vice president of Colombia and the prime minister of Papua New Guinea.

The increasingly isolated Israeli leader's Palestinian counterpart, President Mahmoud Abbas, will also address the General Assembly. Abbas, however, will do so via video, as the US State Department refused to issue him an entry visa.

The broader subjects of Gaza's future and Palestinian statehood will also be topics of discussion. The UK will convene a meeting on Gaza's current and future status, and Saudi Arabia and Norway will host a ministerial meeting to hash out plans for the implementation of the so-called "two-state solution."

Skip next section That's a wrap on Day 2 of the UNGA

That's a wrap on Day 2 of the UNGA

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy blamed Russian President Vladimir Putin for the ongoing war between the countries, calling him "patient zero."

The Ukrainian leader also announced new defense deals with Finland and Australia.

Elsewhere, Syrian leader Ahmed al-Sharaa called for the Israeli occupation of the Golan Heights to end, saying the territory belongs to Syria.

Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez also addressed Israel, calling for what he described as the "genocide" in Gaza to stop.

This comes ahead of a speech by Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu at the UN General Assembly on Thursday.

entries.title: Three-way battle for power in world chess: Who will be elected FIDE president in Samarkand?
entries.summary: The era of Russian presidents is coming to an end at the World Chess Federation (FIDE). Two Germans and one Kazakh are up for election. Among the issues at play are money, Kremlin influence, and unanswered questions.
entries.content:
September 24, 2026

The era of Russian presidents is coming to an end at the World Chess Federation (FIDE). Two Germans and one Kazakh are up for election. Among the issues at play are money, Kremlin influence, and unanswered questions.

"Gens una sumus" ("We are one family") is the motto of the World Chess Federation (FIDE). Yet when officials from some 200 countries gather for their congress in Samarkand on Saturday, September 26, it is not likely to feel like a joyous family reunion.

A new FIDE president is to be elected in Uzbekistan, and a three-way, politically charged race for the post has erupted, with the outcome uncertain. It has been clear since July that the incumbent FIDE president, Arkady Dvorkovich, would not be standing for re-election. The European Union had placed the former Russian deputy prime minister on its sanctions list due to his support for Russia's war of aggression in Ukraine.

Three entrepreneurs vying for the top job

The candidates standing for election are Kazakh billionaire Timur Turlov and two Germans: investor Jan Henric Buettner and entrepreneur Wadim Rosenstein, who is running as the official candidate of the German Chess Federation (DSB).

For the first time in over 30 years, FIDE will not be led by a Russian. Nevertheless, the three contenders repeatedly face two questions: What are their ties to Russia? And where do the millions come from that FIDE uses to finance itself and its competitions? For the Kremlin, chess remains a component of Russia's soft power, and little happens within FIDE without financial backers linked to Russia.

Jan Henric Buettner: The Formula 1 model

Buettner is arguably the best positioned to answer these questions. A native of Hamburg, he has made a name for himself in the chess world through his collaboration with former world champion Magnus Carlsen. The 62-year-old German has no known ties to Moscow that would require explanation. On the contrary: "We are the only team with no connection to Russia," Malcolm Pein — Buettner's candidate for vice president — told DW.

Buettner and his running mate say they intend to reduce reliance on Russian financial backers and make chess commercially successful. Buettner plans to distribute 20% of FIDE's revenue to chess federations worldwide. The former AOL executive looks to Formula 1 motor racing as his model – a vision likely considered too radical by many officials in the chess world. Consequently, Buettner is seen as having only an outside chance of winning.

Timur Turlov: The establishment candidate

The favorite to become FIDE's new president is Timur Turlov. Born in Moscow, he became a Kazakh citizen in 2022 and is one of the wealthiest men in the Central Asian nation. The entrepreneur is considered a close associate of outgoing President Dvorkovich and, by extension, a member of the FIDE establishment. Regarding finances, too, the status quo is likely to remain unchanged under the 38-year-old; after all, Turlov's publicly traded financial firm, Freedom Holding Corp., has been FIDE's main sponsor for many years.

The prospect of Turlov potentially holding the dual roles of FIDE president and major financial backer does not sit well with everyone in the chess community. Furthermore, Freedom Holding Corp. and its CEO are currently on Ukraine's sanctions list. Ukrainian authorities accuse Turlov's company of helping to finance Russia's war of aggression. Press reports also suggest that the US Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) has taken an interest in Turlov's financial firm.

Report: Hamburger Sparkasse closes account

In the spring of 2026, Turlov acquired the Hamburg-based chess software company Chessbase. Shortly thereafter, the German chess news website perlenvombodensee.de reported that the company's principal bank, Hamburger Sparkasse, had closed the Chessbase business account.

Chessbase declined to comment on the matter. Hamburger Sparkasse also did not address the specific case but told DW: "If a business relationship falls under currently existing sanctions – for example, against countries such as Russia, Belarus, or Iran – this may unfortunately result in us being unable to continue specific business relationships."

DW approached Timur Turlov for comment but had received no response by time of publication.

The position of Volodymyr Kovalchuk, vice president of the Ukrainian Chess Federation is clear.

"If Turlov wins the FIDE election and poses a threat to Ukraine's security, then we will push for him to be sanctioned by the EU as well," Kovalchuk told DW.

However, there are now signs of a rapprochement between Turlov and the Ukrainians: Turlov is currently advocating for a Ukrainian official to be elected as a vice president on the FIDE board.

Wadim Rosenstein: Many outstanding questions

The third figure in the mix, Wadim Rosenstein, is also facing intense scrutiny in Ukraine.

"It is absolutely clear that we will not support such a candidate and, should he be elected, will also propose him for sanctions," Kovalchuk said.

Rosenstein was born in 1990 in what is now Ukraine and moved to Germany at the age of nine. In the autumn of 2022, the entrepreneur and amateur chess player began organizing elaborate chess events.

Questions have dogged him ever since, with his business activities and connections to Russia being the primary focus of this scrutiny. According to Rosenstein, the companies within his Düsseldorf-based "WR Group" operate in various sectors, ranging from toilet paper trading and real estate to industrial logistics. Until 2022, a key focus was supporting German companies in regions including Ukraine and Russia, Rosenstein told DW a few months ago. However, he said he was no longer active in Russia; instead positioning himself "globally" across "70 countries," including Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan, and Turkey.

The company in Russia

However, one of the Düsseldorf entrepreneur's remaining companies in Russia has enjoyed economic success in recent years. In July, Rosenstein told DW that these companies were active "only on paper."

It has since become clear that "WR RUS," at least, is anything but a paper tiger. The Moscow-based company has been owned by Rosenstein since 2021. Publicly available data show that "WR RUS's" profit grew from around €300,000 ($341,230) to €1.7 million ($1.93 million) between 2022 and 2025.

Furthermore, records confirm that Rosenstein's German companies – "WR Logistics" and "WR Certification" – collaborated with "WR RUS" through the end of 2023. Documents from "WR RUS" also show a dividend payment equivalent to around €30,000 for the year 2023, which apparently went to him and one of his German companies.

DW again approached Wadim Rosenstein for comment on these matters but received no response by the time of publication of this report.

High-priced players, upscale venues

Since 2022, millions have been poured into Rosenstein's elaborate chess events year after year. The list of Rosenstein's events is long: it includes a top-tier tournament featuring world number one Magnus Carlsen, the 2023 World Team Blitz and Rapid Chess Championship at the prestigious Rheinterrasse in Düsseldorf, and, most recently, the global "WR Women's Chess Tour." A premium venue in Stuttgart has been selected for the tour's finale in November – a location whose name the sponsor is likely to appreciate, Rosenstein Palace.

The FIDE presidential campaign is also costly. On social media, Rosenstein presents himself aboard a private jet during an international campaign tour. According to the Frankfurter Allgemeine newspaper, a portion of the campaign costs is to be covered by Rosenstein's running mate for the vice-presidency – a wealthy real estate entrepreneur from Singapore.

Rosenstein has not disclosed the total cost of his numerous chess activities to date or the exact source of the funds. His company, "WR Logistics," is one of the main sponsors. Rosenstein told DW in July: "I have also used my own funds and brought on partners who trust me."

But who are these partners?

A sponsor that didn't exist

While Rosenstein was preparing his FIDE candidacy in April 2026, he introduced the Düsseldorf-based company "Glotech." He stated he was "proud to introduce our next partner." The sponsor is reportedly providing €250,000 for chess activities in Europe. According to Rosenstein, Glotech is "a true supporter of our vision."

However, according to Glotech Managing Director Evgeni Schukin, this support never existed: "There was no agreement, and we did not make such funds available."

Rosenstein is campaigning primarily on the pledge that FIDE would operate "professionally" under his leadership. On his official website, "WR 2026," he promises transparent and direct communication.

DW approached Rosenstein for comment on the financing of his chess activities, but he did not respond.

Political connections

With the support of the DSB and its president, Paul Meyer-Dunker, Rosenstein has succeeded in establishing himself as a serious challenger to the Turlov, the favorite within FIDE.

The 36-year-old also enjoys support from the world of German politics. In early September, Rosenstein met with Bavarian Interior Minister Joachim Herrmann.

"Joachim Herrmann supports the candidacy of the German applicant Wadim Rosenstein," a subsequently issued statement read.

The Bavarian Interior Ministry told DW that this support related to the "sport-specific focus" of the bid but did not constitute "an assessment of Mr. Rosenstein's private or business activities, nor a prejudgment of any potential reviews by competent authorities."

Online debate cut short

The DSB only learned of the meeting between its FIDE candidate and the Bavarian interior minister after the fact. According to Meyer-Dunker, the DSB supports Rosenstein because he stands for "consistent professionalization" and "greater transparency" within the World Chess Federation. The DSB "has no information regarding Wadim Rosenstein's business activities beyond what has appeared in public reports," Meyer-Dunker said.

Rosenstein had an opportunity to address questions and explain his plans for FIDE's finances in early September. A US chess website had organized an online debate for the candidates. Rosenstein delivered the opening statement; he spoke for just under four minutes, then suddenly exclaimed: "See you in Samarkand!" before cutting the connection.

DW has approached Rosenstein several times to ask why he did not participate in the rest of the discussion regarding FIDE's future. There has been no response to this either.

Dasha Thyssen contributed to this article as a co-author. This article was originally published in German.

entries.title: Ethiopia's military says it killed hundreds of TPLF rebels
entries.summary: The TPLF fought against against the Ethiopian military from 2020 to 2022 in a conflict that saw hundreds of thousands of civilians killed. A resumption of fighting has sparked fears of another brutal war.
entries.content:
Ethiopia

Ethiopia's military says it killed hundreds of TPLF rebels

September 24, 2026

The TPLF fought against against the Ethiopian military from 2020 to 2022 in a conflict that saw hundreds of thousands of civilians killed. A resumption of fighting has sparked fears of another brutal war.

Fighting between Ethiopian troops and the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF) escalated on Thursday, threatening to shatter a fragile 2022 peace deal.

The renewed fighting first broke out in the Tigray Region in northern Ethiopia on Wednesday.

"We are in the situation of full-blown war now," TPLF vice president Amanuel Assefa told AFP news agency.

On Thursday, Ethiopia's military said it "launched a counter-offensive that inflicted heavy personnel and equipment losses on the TPLF."

The military said it killed 272 people among the Tigrayan rebels and wounded some 260 more. These figures could not be independently verified, and there was no breakdown given for soldiers and civilians.

Calls for deescelation

The African Union, the United Nations and other international observers have called for restraint and deescelation.

"I am disappointed to see the leadership of the TPLF, that the United States sanctioned earlier this year, make the poor decision to launch a large-scale offensive today," said Ervin J. Massinga, the US ambassador in Addis Ababa.

"Rejecting dialogue sponsored by the African Union under President Obasanjo and engaging in an unwinnable fight does nothing for the people," he added.

What led to the resumption in fighting?

The TPLF was Ethiopia's dominant political force from 1991 until 2018.

It governed with a coalition of other ethnic-based parties, but critics accused it of creating these parties as loyal opposition to sideline preexisting ethnic movements.

When Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed took office in 2018, he sidelined the TPFL in favor of a government not based on ethnic lines, dominated by his Prosperity Party.

Abiy's early foreign policy saw him repair relations with Ethiopia's former archrival Eritrea — efforts for which he was awarded the Noble Peace Prize in 2019.

But his later determination for landlocked Ethiopia to have access to a seaport was seen as provocative in Eritrea as well in Somalia.

The TPLF then launched a rebellion against Abiy in 2020, spiraling into a two-year war that saw some 500,000 killed due to violence, famine and the collapse of health services.

During that war, Eritrean troops fought alongside Ethiopian federal forces against the TPLF.

Speaking at the UN General Assembly on Wednesday, Ethiopian President Taye Atske Selassie Amde decried "the forces of destruction and mayhem" and "interference in our internal affairs by adversarial elements."

Conflict spreads to Amhara region

Fighting was also reported in the Amhara region in the Ethiopian highlands.

The AFP news agency received reports of fighting around the holy city of Lalibela, home to Ethiopia's ancient, UNESCO-listed rock-hewn churches.

Flights to the popular tourist destination were suspended on Thursday.

The TPLF announced an alliance with Amhara's Fano militia, a former foe that has been waging its own insurgency in the region since 2023.

The Fano militia originally emerged as an opponent of TPFL rule and the two sides still have competing claims over land that was absorbed in to the Amhara region from the Tigray region after the last war.

"The only issue joining them is their opposition to Prosperity Party rule," said Kjetil Tronvoll, a professor of peace and conflict studies at Oslo New ⁠University College.

entries.title: After several difficult years, economists now expect German economy to grow
entries.summary: Germany's economy is growing again, but recovery remains on shaky ground. High government spending is keeping the economy afloat, while energy prices, a shortage of skilled workers and debt continue to weigh on it.
entries.content:
Germany

Is a silver lining on the horizon for Germany's economy?

September 24, 2026

Germany's economy is growing again, but recovery remains on shaky ground. High government spending is keeping the economy afloat, while energy prices, a shortage of skilled workers and debt continue to weigh on it.

After several difficult years, the German economy has regained its footing. Leading economic research institutes now expect the economy to grow by 1.3% in 2026 and by 1.1% next year — significantly more than was forecast back in the spring.

As to the reasons behind this, economists have pointed first and foremost to the global economy. Despite the war in Iran, they say, the economy is proving surprisingly robust.

"This is benefiting the German export sector, and underlying this is also the global boom in artificial intelligence," said Oliver Holtemöller of the Leibniz Institute for Economic Research in Halle during the presentation of the latest report in Berlin.

Because of the blockade of the Strait of Hormuz has cut off supplies from competitors, German companies have seen increased demand from abroad for petroleum and natural gas-based chemical products, for example.

In addition, the construction of AI data centers is driving demand for German companies. Some examples include machinery for energy production and services related to information and communication. Government spending on infrastructure and defense is also a significant driver of this upswing.

However, researchers believe it will not last. For 2028, the institutes expect growth of only 0.4%.

"The drivers of growth will continue to dwindle," said Stefan Kooths of the Kiel-based research institute IfW. High energy prices, a shortage of skilled workers, an aging population and years of low investment by many companies are slowing growth. The institutes therefore warned against misinterpreting the latest positive figures as the beginning of a new economic boom.

Upturn fueled by debt

In this situation, the federal government is also playing a decisive role. The coalition of the conservative Christian Democratic Union (CDU)/Christian Social Union (CSU) and the center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD) has decided to invest heavily in modernizing infrastructure and the Bundeswehr.

In the short term, this additional spending is also helping to generate business for companies and safeguard jobs. At the same time, investments in roads, railways, digital networks and military equipment should strengthen Germany's competitiveness.

Economic analysts agree that this spending has had a positive effect on the economy. The government has been an important engine of growth, especially at a time when consumers are tightening their belts and many companies are postponing investments. But this is also where economists are raising concerns. That's because the spending is financed through debt.

According to forecasts, the government deficit will rise from 4.1% of GDP this year to 4.7% in 2028. At the same time, the government's interest burden will grow. Future budgets will have to allocate an ever-larger share of funds to servicing debt.

"We have two major challenges: one is demographics, and the second is energy security and energy prices," said Holtemöller. In this context, he sharply criticized what the economists see as a lack of clarity regarding "the measures, reforms and regulatory framework" that Germany aims to use to phase out fossil fuels. They noted that a vision for how the energy transition could be carried out in accordance with the Climate Protection Act is "not even vaguely" outlined.

AfD's success scaring off skilled workers

Germany's greatest challenge remains the declining labor force. As the baby boomers enter retirement, the economy is losing millions of workers, and many industries are already complaining of labor shortages. There needs to be greater openness "to the immigration of skilled workers," said Holtemöller.

Referring to the electoral successes of the anti-immigration Alternative for Germany (AfD) — a party that is, in part, right-wing extremist — Holtemöller cited studies indicating that "regions where populist parties are in power tend to have weaker economic growth than other regions." Openness, he emphasized, is the most important factor.

If immigration remains low, the average age of the population will only increase. This will drive up the cost of social security contributions, which in Germany are evenly split between employees and employers. On pension reform, economists are calling for doing away with the option to retire early after 45 years of contributions without any reduction in benefits. They argue that the debate about moving away from this policy is misguided.

Germany's economy in transition

While the government is mobilizing billions, the private sector's momentum is lacking in many places. Investors are being deterred "because they don't know what to expect or what the business landscape looks like here," Kooths explained.

"What companies need now are not new debates but decisions on economic policy," said Helena Melnikov, chief executive of the German Chamber of Commerce and Industry. "This can only be achieved through a decisive course of reform: cutting costs, reducing bureaucracy, streamlining procedures and modernizing infrastructure."

For many decades, Germany was a country with a strong industrial sector. But that sector continues to shrink, with about 15,000 industrial jobs lost every month. Particularly hard-hit are industries such as automotive, mechanical engineering and metals. At the same time, the past two years have seen the emergence of many startups in the fields of digitalization and AI.

But according to economists, these new companies lack support, particularly when it comes to financing. As a result, many are relocating to the US. "We're very good at things like development, patent applications and so on, but the problem is that the ideas developed here end up creating value elsewhere," noted Timo Wollmershäuser of the ifo Institute in Munich.

When asked what could further improve growth prospects in Germany, the researchers pointed to a catalog of reforms that was presented last spring. The proposals include, among other things, a cap on social security contributions and stronger work incentives for older workers. As for the energy transition, the institutes placed greater emphasis on price signals and advocate against taking national action on climate protection without other countries.

Notable criticism was directed at the fuel rebate scheduled to take effect on October 1. Researchers said it amounts to a blanket handout for which there is insufficient fiscal leeway.

The government cannot currently afford such expensive measures, and they are "also economically counterproductive," said Holtemöller of the Leibniz Institute. Cutting fuel taxes would "undermine efforts to reduce demand, which is precisely what is needed when energy supplies are tight."

This article was originally written in German.

entries.title: CNN, MS NOW, Politico regain access to White House
entries.summary: A federal judge has ordered President Trump to restore White House access to CNN, MS NOW and Politico after he banned the media outlets from the premises. Hours later, the media announced they had been granted access.
entries.content:
United States of America

CNN, MS NOW, Politico regain access to White House

September 24, 2026

A federal judge has ordered President Trump to restore White House access to CNN, MS NOW and Politico after he banned the media outlets from the premises. Hours later, the media announced they had been granted access.

CNN, MSNBC, and Politico journalists were allowed back in the White House on Thursday, hours after a federal judge said US President Donald Trump must lift his ban on journalists from CNN, MS NOW and Politico accessing the White House.

The ruling came in response to a lawsuit filed by the news organizations contesting the ban, which was issued on September 18.

In his order, District Judge Tim Kelly said the ban was likely unconstitutional.

Kelly said his order must remain in place for 14 days.

"This is a strong ruling vindicating freedom of the press, due process and the rule of law," Theodore Boutrous Jr., attorney for the outlets, said in a statement emailed to the AP news agency. "We greatly appreciate the court’s swift action."

On Thursday morning, journalists from three affected media outlets were initially denied access. However, later in the day, the media announced they had been granted access to the White House.

What did the judge say about the ban?

Kelly rejected the government's claim that national security concerns promoted the ban.

"The record lacks factual support for defendants’ contention that the revocation of plaintiffs' hard passes will ​in fact protect national security or that national security will be endangered if the court orders their passes reinstated while this litigation ​proceeds," he said.

He pointed out that Trump himself had initially cited only an "alleged lack of truthfulness and negativity" in reporting by the outlets as the reason for the ban.

At a Wednesday hearing, Kelly said two previous rulings from the US Court of Appeals for the ⁠District of ​Columbia Circuit had established that White House press passes can be revoked only after due process.

He said the banned news outlets did not appear to have been given a proper chance to contest the ban.

Kelly, who was nominated by Trump in 2017, ordered a CNN journalist’s access restored in a similar case in 2018.

The ban has led other media outlets, including DW, to take action in solidarity by suspending pooled coverage of Trump events.

Department of Justice support for ban

On Tuesday, the Justice Department had argued in a filing that access ⁠to the White House was a privilege, not ​an entitlement, and that the president had the authority to deny access news organizations.

The outlets, in turn, argued they were singled out because of the content of their coverage and called the ban a "blatant violation" of the First Amendment, which prevents government infringement on freedom of speech and freedom of the press in the United States.

entries.title: Houthi advances in Yemen drive displacement, deepen humanitarian crisis
entries.summary: With more than 132,000 people already displaced by the latest fighting and Houthi territorial gains, Yemen is on the brink of slipping back into a full-fledged humanitarian emergency. DW spoke with people on the ground.
entries.content:
Yemen

Yemen's Saudi-Houthi clash fuels humanitarian crisis

September 24, 2026

With more than 132,000 people already displaced by the latest fighting and Houthi territorial gains, Yemen is on the brink of slipping back into a full-fledged humanitarian emergency. DW spoke with people on the ground.

Mohammed Musleh is still in shock. Following the Houthi capture of the port town of Mokha earlier in September, his family had to flee their home without time to pack.

"We have no idea what will happen now," the 46-year-old told DW. His wife, Muna, is also worried, as the family couldn't bring their personal identification documents. "The Houthis told us to leave, basically immediately. We had no time to take anything," she said.

For now, the family and their two young daughters are staying with relatives in Aden, the largest city controlled by the government in southern Yemen. "We tell our kids in the meantime that we hope to return home soon," the couple said.

Rashad al-Alimi, chairman of the Presidential Council, the leadership body of Yemen’s internationally recognized government, said that recent battlefield changes would not alter the government's goal of restoring state authority nationwide.

However, given the latest advances by the Iran-backed Houthis and their territorial gains in Yemen, a return of the Musleh family to their home in Mokha is unlikely for now.

Since late July, the Iran-backed Houthis have expanded their areas of control from the north and center of the country to much of Yemen's Red Sea coast, seizing territory from forces of the internationally recognized and Saudi-backed government. The conflict continues to escalate, along with an exchange of missile and drone attacks between the Houthis and Saudi Arabia.

The Houthis are currently pushing further into the country toward the strategic Kahboub Mountains. The mountain range is significant as it overlooks areas around the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, a key waterway that had been serving as an alternative route for Saudi oil exports amid Iran's blockade of the nearby Strait of Hormuz.

Staying at home or leaving Taiz?

The mountains are also only around 40 kilometers (25 miles) southwest of Taiz, which is under government control.

Fatima, a mother in Taiz, has been telling her children that the sounds of shelling are from fireworks. "We are scared and we are also worried as gas has already become unavailable and prices are rising. Merchants are no longer coming into Taiz," she told DW, asking not to publish her full name for fear of reprisal.

Rania and her children have also decided to stay at home in Taiz for now. "But we fear that if the Houthis tighten their grip on the city of Taiz, we will find ourselves under siege again," she said. She also doesn't want to use her first name, and vividly recalls the "suffocating blockade of 2015 and 2016, when the entry of food and goods was cut off."

During the previous war between the Iran-aligned Houthi group and the Saudi-backed Yemeni government, which began in 2014 and largely ended with a UN-brokered ceasefire in 2022, Houthi forces blocked most routes into the government-controlled city of Taiz for almost two years. The restrictions on food, medical supplies and humanitarian aid drove up prices and left people on the brink of famine.

Growing displacement numbers

The World Health Organization said this week that at least 674 people have been killed and 2,998 injured since fighting escalated in August. However, due to the ongoing clashes, the death tally may already be higher, as fighting is ongoing.

The conflict has also prompted mass displacement of more than 132,000 people, according to the International Organization for Migration. In recent days, more than 90,000 people found refuge in Aden, Lahj, Abyan and Al Dhale'e governorates and even in Marib, the UN refugee agency's Yemen representative Armen Yedgaryan saidon Tuesday.

He also predicted that intensifying fighting could drive more mass displacement, with growing numbers of people expected to flee to Djibouti, Somalia and other countries, as well as within Yemen.

"Conditions for displaced people are increasingly severe as they arrive at already congested displacement sites in urgent need of shelter, food, clean water, healthcare and protection, placing additional pressure on fragile services and infrastructure," he said.

Even before the latest escalation, more than 5.2 million people were internally displaced in Yemen, and the current fighting is deepening an already dire humanitarian crisis in the country, the UN refugee agency added.

Around 22 million people require humanitarian assistance, including internally displaced people and around 65,000 refugees and asylum-seekers, mainly from Somalia and Ethiopia.

Displaced Yemenis help other displaced Yemenis

"I was in the Al-Kud site, a camp for internally displaced people or IDPs, in Abyan governorate on Sunday," said Alison Bottomley, an advocacy adviser with the Norwegian Refugee Council in Yemen, adding that "317 families have arrived since the fighting began, increasing the number of people from 1,460 to 2,629 people."

However, there is no funding to support them. "These IDPs are surviving purely off the generosity of other IDP families."

She told DW that she met Mustapha, a man who was displaced from his hometown of Mawza seven years ago during the previous war in Yemen. He has been living at the IDP site ever since. "He told us he was hosting 22 families in his shelter, all people from his hometown in Mawza. Together, they share a single latrine. When I asked how they were all eating, he said they share one meal together every other day."

Houthi leader Abdul-Malik al-Houthi, meanwhile, released a video message in which he told Yemenis in western and southern provinces that they are not the target.

However, Yemeni political analyst Hisham Al-Omeisy said these are empty words.

"The Houthis may measure this offensive in kilometers gained and territory seized, but Yemenis are measuring it in homes abandoned, families torn apart, and lives lost," he told DW.

"There is something profoundly cruel about pursuing military gains while ordinary Yemenis are once again being condemned to fear, hunger and displacement," Al-Omeisy said, adding that "the lines on the map may change, but the blood, grief and shattered lives behind those lines belong to real people. Yemen's civilians cannot continue to be treated as collateral damage in the Houthis' pursuit of power."

Edited by: Andreas Illmer

entries.title: Nigeria, US agree to boost mining investment on sidelines of UN General Assembly
entries.summary: On the sidelines of the UN General Assembly, Nigeria and the US inked a new mining deal. Nigeria is home to deposits of lithium, gold, tin, gemstones, iron ore and phosphate.
entries.content:
September 24, 2026

On the sidelines of the UN General Assembly, Nigeria and the US inked a new mining deal. Nigeria is home to deposits of lithium, gold, tin, gemstones, iron ore and phosphate.

Nigeria and the US have agreed to "deepen" American investment in the West African country's mining sector.

The deal was signed on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly in New York City, Nigeria's Minister for Solid Minerals Dele Alake announced on Thursday.

"This is an important step in strengthening Nigeria-US cooperation around our mineral resources, valued at about $700 billion (€796 billion)," Alake said.

"The framework covers geological data and exploration, mineral development and processing, infrastructure, and technical capacity,"he added.

'We want more local processing'

Although known for its vast oil reserves, Nigeria is also home to deposits of lithium, gold, tin, gemstones, iron ore and phosphate.

Lithium, in particular, is in high demand globally as an essential component in the batteries are powering the green energy transition.

Alake said the agreement, which was signed on Wednesday, would be used to identify viable projects. He hinted that local jobs could be created by onshoring the refining of minerals, which until now have largely been exported as ore.

"Nigeria cannot remain a source of raw materials while others capture most of the value," Alake said. "We want more local processing, quality jobs, stronger skills and greater opportunities for Nigerian businesses."

However, these goals come as Nigeria's mining sector remains mired by safety concerns and environmental concerns.

Edited by: Dmytro Hubenko

entries.title: How renewed fighting in Tigray could spread across the Horn of Africa
entries.summary: The fresh hostilities in Ethiopia's Tigray region come after months of growing animosity between rebel forces and the federal government. Horn of Africa expert Martin Plaut warns of possible regional spillover.
entries.content:
Ethiopia

How Tigray's renewed fighting could spread in Horn of Africa

September 24, 2026

The fresh hostilities in Ethiopia's Tigray region come after months of growing animosity between rebel forces and the federal government. Horn of Africa expert Martin Plaut warns of possible regional spillover.

Fighting has erupted again in Ethiopia's northern Tigray region. Tigrayan forces launched a major offensive on September 23, with fighting also reported in the neighboring regions of Afar and Amhara. 

The escalation threatens the fragile peace established by the 2022 Pretoria peace agreement, which ended the previous Tigray war between Ethiopia's federal government in Addis Ababa and the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF).

But the central question is bigger than the return of war to Tigray: could the conflict connect with the wars and rivalries already destabilizing the Horn of Africa and the Red Sea?

Martin Plaut, a British journalist and Horn of Africa expert, argues the conflict could spread beyond Ethiopia's borders.

"If a conflict were to spill over, it is quite possible that a conflict involving Eritrea and Ethiopia could then involve Sudanese forces as well, which could drag the whole region into a war," he told DW in an exclusive interview.

Jalale Getachew Birru, a senior analyst for East Africa at the Armed Conflict Location & Event Data Project (ACLED), also stressed that the conflict cannot be viewed in isolation. ACLED is an independent conflict-monitoring and research organization that collects and analyzes data on political violence and armed conflict around the world.

“The Ethiopia[n] case is not [an] isolated case for the Horn of Africa. It involves the neighboring countries as well, and it's being displayed across the Horn of Africa countries," Birru told DW.

Her assessment points to a broader regional dynamic: Ethiopia's conflict is unfolding alongside shifting alliances and competing interests in neighboring Sudan and Somalia. ACLED's current analysis likewise places the renewed Tigray conflict within a wider pattern of instability across the Horn of Africa.

The risk is not based on a single regional alliance. It comes from the fact that several conflicts are already geographically and politically connected, Birru noted.

African Union urges restraint

The African Union (AU) has also expressed deep concern about the possibility of further destabilization.

In a statement on September 23, AU Commission Chairperson Mahmoud Ali Youssouf warned that new political and military alliances risk reversing the progress made since 2020.

The AU called for an immediate end to actions that could escalate tensions, renewed direct talks under the Pretoria agreement and restraint by Ethiopia's neighbors. It also tasked former Nigerian President Olusegun Obasanjo, the AU's high representative for the Horn of Africa, with supporting diplomatic efforts.

The AU's intervention reflects concerns that the crisis could have wider regional implications, including the possibility that it could interact with conflicts beyond Ethiopia's borders.

Old enemies, new alliances

The TPLF recently joined six other Ethiopian armed groups in an alliance seeking to remove Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed's government. Among them is the Amhara Fano movement, which fought against the TPLF during the previous war.

The alliance is not a unified military force, and its members have different political objectives and territorial interests. But its formation could leave the Ethiopian government facing several fronts at once.

The fighting in Afar, a northeastern Ethiopian region bordering Eritrea and Djibouti, is particularly significant. The region contains the main transport corridor linking landlocked Ethiopia to Djibouti, through which much of Ethiopia's international trade passes. Sustained fighting there could therefore threaten a vital economic lifeline.

And beyond Afar lies Eritrea.

Eritrea's potential role

During the 2020–2022 Tigray war, Eritrean troops fought alongside Ethiopian federal forces against the TPLF. Since then, relations between Addis Ababa and Asmara, Eritrea's capital, have deteriorated. Ethiopia's ambitions for access to the Red Sea have added to Eritrea's security concerns.

"The war could certainly escalate, and Eritrea could become involved," Plaut said.

Ethiopia has accused Eritrea of supporting armed groups opposed to the government, while Asmara has denied such allegations. The extent of any direct Eritrean involvement remains difficult to establish independently.

Sudan: Where conflicts could collide

Sudan has been at war since 2023 between the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) and the Rapid Support Forces (RSF). The conflict has drawn in regional powers and created one of the world's largest humanitarian crises.

Plaut argues that Ethiopia and Eritrea are already indirectly involved on opposing sides.

"The Ethiopians are on the side of the RSF and Hemedti," he said, referring to its commander Mohamed Hamdan Dagalo. "There has been strong evidence that there is a base in western Ethiopia which is supplying and training RSF fighters," Plaut added. DW has not independently verified that claim.

The United Arab Emirates (UAE) has faced allegations of supporting the RSF, which it denies. Plaut identifies Eritrea, Egypt and Saudi Arabia as supporting the Sudanese Armed Forces.

"So both Eritrea and Ethiopia are already playing a role, indirectly, in the war," he said.

If Ethiopia and Eritrea were to enter direct hostilities, Sudan's rival forces could have incentives to exploit the new situation, Plaut said. Fighting could put additional pressure on Sudan's eastern frontier and alter supply routes and military calculations.

Plaut sees the danger of a chain reaction: "Because you have the UAE backing the RSF and you have the Saudis backing the Eritreans and the Sudanese Armed Forces, this could all multiply and you could get one conflict leading into another."

"So the whole thing becomes a generalized conflict in the region," he said.

Red Sea connection

The Bab el-Mandeb Strait, one of the world's most important shipping choke points, connects the Red Sea with the Gulf of Aden and the Indian Ocean.

Eritrea and Djibouti lie on its western side, Yemen on the eastern side. The war in Yemen has already shown how insecurity around the Red Sea can disrupt international shipping and draw in outside powers.

Eritrea's location and its control of the port of Assab give it strategic importance far beyond Tigray. Any major deterioration in Ethiopia-Eritrea relations could therefore affect the wider security architecture of the Red Sea.

Saudi Arabia and the UAE have also developed extensive political, economic and security interests across the Horn of Africa. Their interests overlap in some areas but diverge in others, particularly over Sudan.

Danger is escalation, not inevitability

None of this means that a regional war is inevitable. There is no evidence of a single military alliance stretching from Tigray to the Gulf. Ethiopia's armed groups have competing interests, Eritrea may avoid direct intervention, and Sudan's warring parties have their own priorities.

But conflicts do not need a common command structure to become interconnected.

The Tigray war killed hundreds of thousands of people and displaced millions. The Pretoria agreement stopped the large-scale fighting, but many of the political and territorial disputes underlying the conflict remained unresolved.

Today, Tigray is again at war while Ethiopia faces several armed movements, Eritrea is a potential military actor, and Sudan is already engulfed in civil war.

Plaut warns that the humanitarian consequences could again be severe.

"There's certainly a danger of this becoming an extremely bloody conflict," he told DW. "After all, 600,000 people died in the last one in Tigray."

But he does not predict that the previous death toll will necessarily be exceeded. "Let's hope that it doesn't go in that direction," he said.

Edited by: Keith Walker
